name: Soul patch

card.summary: A small tuft of hair under the lower lip, grown for a minimalist, accented chin that draws attention to the lip and jaw area without a full beard.

quick.overview:
A soul patch is a small patch of facial hair between the lower lip and the chin. It is a low-commitment facial hair style that adds definition to the lower face for people who prefer a clean-shaven look otherwise.

It has a long history, from 17th-century European portraits to 1950s jazz musicians, beatniks, and a 1990s revival.
quick.how: People grow the patch and keep the surrounding cheeks, chin and upper lip shaved, trimming it short with clippers and a razor to keep its edges defined. Maintenance every few days is typical.
quick.risks: The style has no known medical risks beyond ordinary skin issues in the area, such as a published case report of dermatitis affecting the soul-patch hair.

lead: A soul patch, also called a mouche, is a small patch of facial hair between the lower lip and the chin.[1] People wear it as a minimal alternative to a goatee or beard, adding visual interest to the lower face.

Wikipedia traces the style to 17th-century Europe, citing a c. 1625 Frans Hals portrait, and to African-American jazz musicians and beatniks of the 1950s and 1960s.[1] It was revived in the early 1990s partly through Luke Perry's character in Buffy the Vampire Slayer and gained popularity in late-1990s mall goth and nu-metal scenes.[1]
Grokipedia attributes the look to Dizzy Gillespie and says he found it comfortable under a trumpet mouthpiece; Wikipedia marks a similar flute claim as uncited.[1][2]

chain: Grow a small tuft below the lip
Keep the rest of the face shaved
angle.text: The soul patch adds a small focal point beneath the lip for people who prefer minimal facial hair. It suits those who want some chin hair without a full goatee or beard.

paras: The patch sits just below the lower lip on the midline, separate from the mustache and the cheeks.[2] Grokipedia describes a typical size of about 2 cm wide and 1 cm tall, trimmed to a few millimetres.[2]

The style appears in 17th-century Dutch painting and was common among African-American jazz musicians in the 1950s and 1960s, spreading to beatniks and artists. Frank Zappa wore one from the early 1960s.[1]
The earliest recorded use of the term "soul patch" is dated to 1986 by Merriam-Webster, according to Wikipedia, though other accounts give earlier dates.[1][2]
Grokipedia describes trimming the patch with clippers and defining the edges with a razor, shaving surrounding areas every few days.[2]
A 2024 case report in SKINmed described a 20-year-old man with dermatitis affecting his soul-patch hair that was initially treated as herpes simplex before dermatology review.[3]
No studies found. A single case report describes dermatitis in the soul-patch area.[3]

timeline.event: Frans Hals portrait shows a similar tuft.[1]
